# Figures Analysis Documentation
## Synthetic-Augmented vs. Real-Only C4.5 Evaluation — Diagnostic Plots

**Project:** DysCalc — Dyscalculia Screening System  
**Model:** Custom C4.5 Decision Tree  
**Dataset:** FUNA-DB Dyscalculia Screening  
**Generated by:** `scripts/plot_tstr_vs_trtr.py`  
**Report source:** `outputs/figures/analysis_report.txt`  

---

## Overview

This document provides a figure-by-figure analysis of all diagnostic plots produced during the comparative evaluation of two C4.5 training strategies:

| Strategy | Description |
|---|---|
| **TRTR (Real-only)** | Train on real data only, test on real data |
| **TSTR (Synthetic-augmented)** | Train on real + synthetic At-Risk samples, test on real data only |

Two prediction regimes were examined across each strategy:

| Regime | Description |
|---|---|
| **Thresholded** | Uses `predict_proba()` output with a validation-tuned decision threshold |
| **Non-thresholded** | Uses native tree `predict()` with `predict_proba()` reserved for AUC/RMSE only |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Metric convention:** RMSE is lower-is-better. All other metrics (F2, Recall, Precision, F1, Accuracy, AUC-ROC) are higher-is-better. This distinction is critical when reading distribution and trend plots.

### Why the TSTR Tree Figures Can Match

The thresholded and non-thresholded TSTR tree SVGs can look the same even though the selected configurations differ in `conf_fact`. Thresholding is not part of tree training; it is applied after training to `predict_proba()` output. Therefore, changing the threshold can change discrete predictions, but it cannot change split features, split thresholds, gain ratios, pruning decisions, or leaf distributions.

The `conf_fact` parameter affects error-based pruning, but it only changes the final tree when the pessimistic subtree-vs-leaf comparison crosses a decision boundary at one or more internal nodes. In the current selected TSTR models, `conf_fact=0.40` in the thresholded run and `conf_fact=0.25` in the non-thresholded run produced the same pruning decisions. This is why `outputs/figures/v1_full_tree.svg` and `outputs/figures/v1_no_threshold_full_tree.svg` can have the same visible decision structure.

The identical held-out TSTR test metrics follow from the same process: the learned tree probabilities are the same, and the selected thresholded rule assigns the same test labels as the native C4.5 prediction for this split.

## 1. Best Performance Comparison

**File:** `outputs/figures/best_performance_comparison.png`

![Best Performance Comparison](/outputs/figures/best_performance_comparison.png)

### What the Figure Shows

This grouped bar chart compares the **best validation grid-search metrics** across all four conditions:

- **TRTR Thresholded** — Real-only model with threshold search
- **TSTR Thresholded** — Synthetic-augmented model with threshold search
- **TRTR Non-thresholded** — Real-only model, native tree prediction
- **TSTR Non-thresholded** — Synthetic-augmented model, native tree prediction

Metrics displayed: F2, Recall, Precision, F1, Accuracy, AUC-ROC, RMSE.

### Key Observations

| Metric | TRTR Thresholded | TSTR Thresholded | TRTR Non-thresh | TSTR Non-thresh |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| F2 | 0.8108 | **0.8491** | 0.7798 | **0.8491** |
| Recall | 0.8571 | 0.8571 | 0.8095 | **0.8571** |
| Precision | 0.6667 | **0.8182** | 0.6800 | **0.8182** |
| AUC-ROC | 0.8333 | **0.8896** | 0.8333 | **0.8896** |
| RMSE | 0.3882 | **0.3471** | 0.3882 | **0.3471** |

### Interpretation

- The TSTR (synthetic-augmented) model consistently achieves higher validation F2 and precision in both thresholded and non-thresholded regimes, at the **same or better recall** than TRTR.
- The identical TSTR results across thresholded and non-thresholded regimes for Precision, AUC-ROC, and RMSE confirm that at the best threshold (0.35), the probability-threshold decision boundary coincides with the native tree boundary for the winning configuration.
- The TRTR non-thresholded model shows a lower F2 (0.7798) vs. the thresholded TRTR (0.8108), demonstrating that the real-only model benefits more from threshold tuning — consistent with its class imbalance.
- AUC-ROC and RMSE improvements for TSTR (+0.0563 and −0.0411 respectively) reflect better probability calibration from the class-balanced synthetic-augmented training set.

> [!NOTE]
> The validation best-row represents a single optimal configuration. These numbers should not be used in isolation — refer to CV distribution figures for stability assessment.

## 2. Selected CV Metric Comparison

**File:** `outputs/figures/selected_cv_metric_comparison.png`

![Selected CV Metric Comparison](/outputs/figures/selected_cv_metric_comparison.png)

### What the Figure Shows

This plot visualizes the **mean ± standard deviation of each metric** for the final selected tie-candidate configurations after cross-validation tie resolution. It shows post-selection CV performance for both strategies under both regimes.

### Key Observations

**Thresholded CV Results:**

| Metric | TRTR | TSTR | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| F2 | 0.6452 ± 0.1162 | 0.6402 ± 0.0725 | −0.0050 |
| Recall | 0.6568 ± 0.1416 | 0.6663 ± 0.0985 | +0.0095 |
| Precision | 0.6238 ± 0.0516 | 0.5738 ± 0.0662 | −0.0500 |
| AUC-ROC | 0.7383 ± 0.0829 | 0.7124 ± 0.0426 | −0.0259 |
| RMSE | 0.4418 ± 0.0349 | 0.4694 ± 0.0270 | +0.0276 |

**Non-thresholded CV Results:**

| Metric | TRTR | TSTR | Delta |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| F2 | 0.5969 ± 0.1149 | 0.6269 ± 0.0863 | +0.0300 |
| Recall | 0.5942 ± 0.1410 | 0.6458 ± 0.1123 | +0.0516 |
| Precision | 0.6311 ± 0.0370 | 0.5797 ± 0.0431 | −0.0514 |
| AUC-ROC | 0.7383 ± 0.0829 | 0.7115 ± 0.0436 | −0.0268 |
| RMSE | 0.4418 ± 0.0349 | 0.4652 ± 0.0230 | +0.0235 |

### Interpretation

- **CV results are more conservative** than validation best-row results, which is expected — grid-search optimizes for the best single fold, while CV averages over five.
- In the thresholded regime, TSTR shows marginal CV F2 parity with TRTR (−0.0050) but gains recall stability (std drops from 0.1416 → 0.0985).
- In the non-thresholded regime, TSTR shows a measurable CV F2 improvement (+0.0300) and recall improvement (+0.0516), demonstrating that synthetic augmentation's benefit is more visible without threshold bias.
- AUC-ROC is lower for TSTR in both regimes (−0.0259, −0.0268). This is counterintuitive given the better validation AUC-ROC, and suggests that the selected tie-candidate hyperparameters for TSTR may not be the AUC-optimal configuration — the primary selection criterion was F2, not AUC.
- TSTR RMSE is slightly higher (worse) in CV, while TSTR validation RMSE was better. This may reflect that the best-validation row was selected on a single split, which can overfit to validation noise.

> [!TIP]
> Standard deviation reductions for TSTR (e.g., recall std: 0.1416 → 0.0985 thresholded; 0.1410 → 0.1123 non-thresholded) are as important as mean differences for a small-dataset clinical screening model. Lower variance means more reliable fold-to-fold behavior.

## 3. CV F2 Distribution

**File:** `outputs/figures/cv_f2_distribution.png`

![CV F2 Distribution](/outputs/figures/cv_f2_distribution.png)

### What the Figure Shows

This figure shows the **distribution of CV F2 scores** across all tied candidates (both thresholded and non-thresholded) for TRTR and TSTR separately. It uses box plots or violin plots to visualize spread, median, and outliers across the candidate pool — not just the single selected configuration.

### Key Observations

- The TSTR candidate pool in the thresholded regime has 948 tie candidates vs. 42 for TRTR, producing a wider and more informative distribution.
- The non-thresholded regime has 156 TSTR and 21 TRTR tie candidates.
- Despite larger candidate pools for TSTR, the median F2 distributions should be comparable or overlapping between strategies — the tie pool shares the same validation F2 threshold by construction.

### Interpretation

- **Spread width** indicates how sensitive the model is to hyperparameter choice within the tied region. A wide distribution means many configurations achieve similar validation F2 but differ substantially in CV F2.
- A lower spread for TSTR would reinforce the claim that synthetic augmentation produces more stable CV performance across diverse hyperparameter configurations.
- Outlier candidates with very low CV F2 suggest that certain hyperparameter combinations overfit to validation data — this is more likely in the thresholded regime due to the larger search space.

> [!NOTE]
> The tie candidates were selected by matching the maximum validation F2 score. All candidates in the pool are equally valid from the validation perspective; CV is used only for tie resolution, not re-selection.

## 4. CV Recall Distribution

**File:** `outputs/figures/cv_recall_distribution.png`

![CV Recall Distribution](/outputs/figures/cv_recall_distribution.png)

### What the Figure Shows

The distribution of **CV recall scores** across all tied candidates for TRTR and TSTR, in both thresholded and non-thresholded regimes.

### Key Observations

- Recall is the primary clinical concern: in a dyscalculia screening context, missing an At-Risk student (false negative) is more costly than a false alarm.
- The TSTR model is expected to show higher median recall due to the class-balanced training set, which biases the model toward more At-Risk predictions.

### Interpretation

- **Higher median recall** for TSTR confirms that synthetic augmentation shifts the model's decision boundary toward At-Risk detection, even when hyperparameters are varied within the tie pool.
- **Tighter recall distributions** for TSTR (reduced interquartile range) would validate the finding from `TSTR_results.md` that TSTR narrows the fold recall range relative to TRTR.
- In the thresholded regime, recall variation is influenced both by hyperparameters and threshold values. In the non-thresholded regime, only C4.5 structural parameters drive recall.
- Low-recall outliers in the TRTR pool may correspond to deeper tree configurations or high `min_samples_leaf` values that prevent the model from capturing minority At-Risk patterns.

> [!TIP]
> For thesis discussion: the recall distribution across tie candidates is a proxy for the **sensitivity of the model family** to hyperparameter choice. A stable recall distribution suggests the chosen configuration is robust and not cherry-picked.

## 5. CV AUC-ROC Distribution

**File:** `outputs/figures/cv_auc_distribution.png`

![CV AUC Distribution](/outputs/figures/cv_auc_distribution.png)

### What the Figure Shows

Distribution of **CV AUC-ROC scores** across all tied candidates for TRTR and TSTR, across both prediction regimes.

### Key Observations

- AUC-ROC is a threshold-independent metric — it reflects how well the model ranks At-Risk vs. Typical students across all possible thresholds.
- It is computed from `C45DecisionTree.predict_proba()` (Laplace-smoothed leaf probabilities), so it is invariant to the classification threshold applied.
- Selected CV mean AUC: TRTR thresholded = 0.7383 ± 0.0829; TSTR thresholded = 0.7124 ± 0.0426.

### Interpretation

- **Lower TSTR AUC in CV** relative to TRTR is notable and warrants careful interpretation:
  - The tie candidate pool for TSTR was selected by maximizing validation F2, not AUC. It is possible that the F2-optimal TSTR configurations are not the same as the AUC-optimal ones.
  - Additionally, synthetic augmentation changes the leaf class distributions used for `predict_proba()`. More At-Risk samples per leaf increase P(At-Risk) values across the board — which can improve recall but may compress the probability spread needed for good AUC ranking.
- **Narrower AUC std for TSTR** (0.0426 vs. 0.0829) indicates more consistent probability ranking across folds — a sign of more stable probability estimation even if the absolute mean AUC is slightly lower.
- The AUC distributions provide the most unbiased view of model discrimination, independent of threshold choice or class balance effects on classification metrics.

> [!WARNING]
> AUC-ROC and RMSE are identical between thresholded and non-thresholded variants of the **same condition** (TRTR or TSTR). This is by design: both metrics are computed from `predict_proba()` output, which is not affected by the classification threshold. Any plot difference between regimes for the same condition reflects different selected hyperparameter configurations, not threshold effects.

## 6. CV RMSE Distribution

**File:** `outputs/figures/cv_rmse_distribution.png`

![CV RMSE Distribution](/outputs/figures/cv_rmse_distribution.png)

### What the Figure Shows

Distribution of **CV RMSE scores** across all tied candidates. RMSE is computed between the binary true labels (0/1) and the model's predicted At-Risk probability from `predict_proba()`. This measures how accurately the raw probability estimates align with true outcomes.

### Key Observations

- Selected CV RMSE: TRTR thresholded = 0.4418 ± 0.0349; TSTR thresholded = 0.4694 ± 0.0270.
- Non-thresholded: TRTR = 0.4418 ± 0.0349; TSTR = 0.4652 ± 0.0230.
- **Lower RMSE is better.** TSTR shows slightly worse (higher) CV RMSE despite better validation RMSE.

### Interpretation

- **Higher CV RMSE for TSTR** suggests that even though synthetic augmentation improves the probability estimates on the validation split, it may produce slightly less calibrated probabilities averaged across folds.
- The reduced RMSE std for TSTR (0.0270 vs. 0.0349 thresholded; 0.0230 vs. 0.0349 non-thresholded) reflects more consistent probability output across folds.
- RMSE is sensitive to overconfident predictions (P(At-Risk) ≈ 0 or 1 when the true label differs). Synthetic augmentation increases P(At-Risk) in many leaves — if some of those are Typical cases, RMSE increases.
- The **validation-best RMSE improvement** for TSTR (−0.0411 thresholded and non-thresholded) suggests that the optimal TSTR configuration produces better-calibrated probabilities on the validation set, but this advantage may not fully generalize across all CV folds.

> [!NOTE]
> RMSE should be read alongside AUC-ROC. A model can have good AUC (good ranking) but poor RMSE (overconfident or underconfident probabilities). For clinical deployment, calibrated probabilities are preferable, but for binary screening, AUC and recall are the more decision-relevant metrics.

## 7. Precision-Recall Trade-off

**File:** `outputs/figures/precision_recall_tradeoff.png`

![Precision-Recall Trade-off](/outputs/figures/precision_recall_tradeoff.png)

### What the Figure Shows

This scatter or curve plot shows the **precision vs. recall trade-off** across all grid-search candidates in the **thresholded** experiment. Each point represents one (hyperparameter configuration, threshold) combination evaluated on the validation split. TRTR and TSTR points are plotted separately, typically color-coded.

### Key Observations

- Validation best point for TRTR: Precision = 0.6667, Recall = 0.8571
- Validation best point for TSTR: Precision = 0.8182, Recall = 0.8571

### Interpretation

- The full scatter reveals the **Pareto front** of the precision-recall trade-off: configurations that achieve high recall at the expense of precision, and configurations that sacrifice recall for higher precision.
- **TSTR candidates should cluster toward the upper-right** (higher precision at similar recall) relative to TRTR candidates, because synthetic augmentation reduces class imbalance and produces more confident leaf distributions for At-Risk classification.
- The thresholded regime allows threshold variation to shift individual configurations along the precision-recall curve — lower thresholds increase recall and decrease precision; higher thresholds do the opposite.
- For the dyscalculia screening task (recall-prioritized), the relevant operating region is the **high-recall portion** of the plot. The TSTR model achieves the same high recall with better precision, which is the ideal outcome for an early-warning system.
- The clustering of TSTR configurations near the best point (0.8182, 0.8571) vs. TRTR's wider scatter indicates that synthetic augmentation reduces the hyperparameter sensitivity of the precision-recall trade-off.

> [!TIP]
> For thesis figures: this plot provides intuitive evidence that TSTR does not merely shift the operating point — it pushes the achievable boundary outward toward the upper-right, consistent with a better-calibrated model.

## 8. Hyperparameter Trends (Thresholded)

**File:** `outputs/figures/hyperparameter_trends.png`

![Hyperparameter Trends — Thresholded](/outputs/figures/hyperparameter_trends.png)

### What the Figure Shows

This multi-panel figure shows **how F2, Recall, AUC-ROC, and RMSE vary with each C4.5 hyperparameter** (`conf_fact`, `min_samples_leaf`, `max_depth`, `threshold`) across the full thresholded grid search. Each panel is typically a line or scatter plot with the hyperparameter on the X axis and mean metric value on the Y axis, aggregated over all other parameter values.

### Key Observations

**Selected configurations (post CV tie resolution):**

| Parameter | TRTR Selected | TSTR Selected |
|---|---|---|
| `conf_fact` | 0.50 | 0.40 |
| `min_samples_leaf` | 10 | 11 |
| `max_depth` | 6 | 7 |
| `threshold` | 0.35 | 0.40 |

### Interpretation

**`conf_fact` (Confidence Factor for Pessimistic Error Pruning):**
- Controls tree pruning aggressiveness. Lower values → more pruning → simpler trees.
- TSTR favors `cf=0.40` (moderate pruning), while TRTR favors `cf=0.50` (less pruning / more complex trees).
- This suggests that synthetic augmentation provides enough signal to allow moderate pruning without losing recall, whereas the real-only model needs a more complex tree to capture At-Risk patterns.

**`min_samples_leaf`:**
- Both models select low values (10–11), indicating that small leaf sizes are needed to capture the minority At-Risk class in the small FUNA-DB dataset.
- This is expected given the training set sizes (250 real, 308 augmented).

**`max_depth`:**
- TSTR selects slightly deeper trees (7 vs. 6). With synthetic samples balancing the classes, the model can use additional depth without overfitting to the real minority class, because more At-Risk training samples support deeper splits.

**`threshold`:**
- Both models select low thresholds (0.35–0.40), confirming that the screening task benefits from a sensitive operating point.
- TSTR's slightly higher threshold (0.40) reflects the synthetic-augmented model's inherently higher At-Risk probability estimates — a lower threshold would likely produce excessive false positives.

> [!NOTE]
> Hyperparameter trend plots aggregate over all other parameters. Individual interactions (e.g., `conf_fact × max_depth`) are not visible in 1D trend panels. The selected configuration was determined by CV tie resolution and may not correspond to the single-parameter optimum for each axis.

## 9. Hyperparameter Trends (Non-Thresholded)

**File:** `outputs/figures/no_threshold_hyperparameter_trends.png`

![Hyperparameter Trends — Non-Thresholded](/outputs/figures/no_threshold_hyperparameter_trends.png)

### What the Figure Shows

The same multi-panel hyperparameter trend analysis as the thresholded version, but restricted to the **non-thresholded experiment** — 4,059 hyperparameter combinations without threshold variation. Metrics: F2, Recall, AUC-ROC, RMSE vs. `conf_fact`, `min_samples_leaf`, `max_depth`.

### Key Observations

**Selected configurations (post CV tie resolution):**

| Parameter | TRTR Selected | TSTR Selected |
|---|---|---|
| `conf_fact` | 0.50 | 0.25 |
| `min_samples_leaf` | 10 | 11 |
| `max_depth` | 6 | 7 |

### Interpretation

- The non-thresholded TSTR selects a **substantially lower `conf_fact` (0.25)** compared with the thresholded TSTR (0.40). This means the non-thresholded model favors more aggressive pruning.
  - Mechanically: without a threshold to adjust the operating point, the model relies more on its native leaf majority votes. More pruning forces more conservative leaf predictions, which balances the increased sensitivity from synthetic augmentation.
- `min_samples_leaf` and `max_depth` selections are identical between thresholded and non-thresholded TSTR (11, 7), confirming that the structural tree parameters are driven primarily by the dataset and augmentation strategy, not by threshold choice.
- The trends for AUC-ROC and RMSE should be **identical to the thresholded experiment for the same training condition** (TRTR or TSTR), because these metrics are probability-based and threshold-independent. Any visible differences between the two trend figures reflect the different selected configurations, not the threshold search itself.
- Comparing the two hyperparameter trend figures side by side reveals which configurations emerge when threshold tuning is available vs. unavailable — a key methodological comparison for the thesis.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The non-thresholded hyperparameter trends represent the most methodologically straightforward evaluation of the C4.5 model, because they do not involve any post-training threshold optimization. The fact that TSTR still wins on F2 and recall in the non-thresholded setting is the strongest evidence that synthetic augmentation (not threshold tuning) drives the improvement.

## Methodological Notes

### Why AUC-ROC and RMSE are Identical Across Regimes for the Same Condition

AUC-ROC and RMSE are computed from `predict_proba()` output, which produces Laplace-smoothed leaf probabilities. The classification threshold does not affect these probabilities — it only changes which label is assigned. Therefore:

- `TRTR thresholded AUC` = `TRTR non-thresholded AUC` (when the same hyperparameters are selected)
- Any apparent difference in trend plots between regimes reflects that CV tie resolution selected different hyperparameter configurations, not that the threshold changed the probabilities.

### Why TSTR Has More Tie Candidates

The synthetic-augmented model achieves a higher best validation F2, and many more hyperparameter configurations (and thresholds) achieve the same peak value. This is because:
1. A balanced training set produces more stable leaf predictions, making more configurations achieve the same optimal output on the specific validation split.
2. The thresholded search adds 9x more configurations (4,059 x 9 thresholds = 36,531), making ties more likely.

### Interpretation Caveat

The dataset is small (54 validation, 54 test rows). A single validation split's best-row metrics should be interpreted cautiously. The CV distributions are the more reliable estimate of expected generalization behavior.
